stories.title: Airlock pairs coding-agent policies with an audit collector
stories.summary: An early agent-management framework combines versioned permissions, selected action records and a shadow mode for observing policy behavior.
body: Airlock is an early framework for managing autonomous coding agents through policies kept in version control. Its creator describes the project in a first-party Show HN announcement, including an OpenTelemetry collector that stores selected agent actions for audits. The intended problem is managing agent permissions and accountability across a business rather than configuring each developer’s local assistant.

First, an agent run proves its identity using a GitHub-issued identity token. Airlock exchanges that proof for a short-lived GitHub token restricted to the repositories and permissions in the agent’s role file. Teams can then set a repository’s autonomy level and apply stricter overrides to individual files. A shadow mode lets them observe how the framework would behave before enabling it.

The audit collector records a subset of actions, so the announcement does not establish complete execution coverage. Prompt storage that only customers can decrypt remains exploratory. The creator says the schemas and reusable GitHub actions are public, while opening the backplane’s source is planned after further development.
stories.takeaway: Teams piloting fleet policies should test which agent actions reach the audit record and which remain outside its coverage.

stories.title: ClickHouse gives investigation agents managed access to telemetry
stories.summary: A managed observability beta exposes the same logs, metrics and traces to engineers and investigation agents.
body: ClickHouse Observability is a managed service for investigating logs, metrics and traces using the open-source ClickStack interface. Its public beta removes database administration from the default setup. The announcement explicitly targets engineers and their investigation agents, whose queries can create changing capacity demands.

First, a team creates a service and sends existing OpenTelemetry data to its managed ingestion endpoint. ClickHouse handles ingestion, schemas and storage. Engineers explore the records in ClickStack, while agents access the same telemetry through its Model Context Protocol server, an interface for calling investigation tools. Those tools search logs and follow traces; SQL supports additional analysis.

A separate private preview, Observability Apps, lets agents generate investigation screens over live data. The publisher says generated code runs in a sandbox, with read-only queries using the viewer’s database permissions. These are separate availability stages. During beta, ClickHouse plans further work on automatic scaling and schema optimization.
stories.takeaway: Teams giving agents production telemetry access should verify query permissions and follow findings back to the underlying records.

stories.title: Elastic checks an investigation agent’s answer against traces and a query
stories.summary: A fault-injection walkthrough follows an agent’s diagnosis to a failing operation, then checks its scope with a direct query.
body: Elastic AI Agent investigates production telemetry through a conversational interface. An Elastic walkthrough tests its findings against application performance monitoring records in an instrumented demonstration shop. A checkout alert appears upstream of an injected payment fault, so the investigation must separate the visible symptom from the failing service.

First, the authors attach the alert to the agent’s conversation. Its answer points to payment failures, but expresses uncertainty about whether a particular customer tier is affected. They then open the service map and drill through a transaction into a failing span, the record of one operation within a trace.

Finally, a direct Elasticsearch Query Language query checks the suspected scope: 80 of 138 gold-tier charges failed, while other tiers did not. This is a controlled demonstration with injected faults, not a production incident or a general accuracy benchmark. The article also warns that the agent’s answers vary between runs.
stories.takeaway: When using agents for incident diagnosis, retain a path from each proposed cause to trace evidence and a reproducible scope check.

stories.title: HoneyHive explains how to keep tool calls linked across MCP boundaries
stories.summary: A tracing guide separates request identity, tool failures and sensitive payloads when instrumenting Model Context Protocol calls.
body: Model Context Protocol, or MCP, connects agents to tools and data. HoneyHive’s engineering guide explains how to trace requests across its client and server so a failed tool call stays linked to the agent run. A shared connection alone cannot identify that run because unrelated requests can be interleaved.

First, the client places trace context in the request’s metadata, allowing the server to connect its operation record to the caller. This works across both local process communication and HTTP. Next, instrumentation records the method, relevant tool name, timing and error type. A tool can fail inside an otherwise successful protocol response, so that result needs its own error classification.

The guide cautions that OpenTelemetry’s MCP conventions remain in development and instrumentation may not emit the expected fields. Tool arguments and results are optional, potentially sensitive data. HoneyHive describes its automatic instrumentation as experimental and recommends explicit tracing decorators for production; its MCP guide does not itself document cross-service propagation.
stories.takeaway: Inspect emitted records and test propagation across an actual client-server call before relying on an MCP dashboard.

stories.title: Langfuse keeps monitor alerts and score views closer to their evidence
stories.summary: Release fixes preserve alert filters in observation links and correct several evaluation-score display and query cases.
body: Langfuse is an AI observability platform that collects application traces and evaluation scores. Its stable release includes changes to the evidence available when operators investigate a monitor alert or review quality results. These fixes address the connection between a notification and its underlying records, along with score visibility.

First, monitor alert messages now include the measured value and its unit. The observation link also carries the alert’s filters, preserving the selection used by the notification. These are distinct changes: one makes the message more informative, while the other keeps the investigation link aligned with its criteria.

Then, score-related fixes load score configurations for read-only users and display trace-level correction scores in the individual trace view. A dashboard query fix excludes deleted scores in a join when its normal finalization step is skipped. The release notes identify these implementation changes but provide no measured improvement in investigation time or evaluation accuracy.
stories.takeaway: Langfuse operators should compare a known alert’s filters with its linked observations and verify score visibility using a read-only account.
